stories.take:
Dylan Larkin has widened his list of acceptable trade destinations to 10 teams, per ESPN, which reports he told the Red Wings he would go to at least seven more clubs than his original three. Daily Faceoff says he loosened the list to help get a deal done, and The Athletic notes he has scored 30-plus goals in five straight seasons with Detroit.

The numbers so far this season say the Red Wings aren't losing a player who is carrying them. Larkin has 1 goal and 3 points in 6 games, and his own expected goals (the quality of his chances, tallied as goals) sit at 1.51, so he is 0.51 goals below what his chances should have produced. That looks like a small-sample dip, not a decline. At 5-on-5, DET holds 51.19% of the expected goals with him on the ice, a touch better than the team's 49.8% overall, though the team's results are 1.27 points of share worse with him on the ice than off. DET is 3-3-2, and its goalies have saved 3.8 goals more than expected, which is propping up a record that its finishing (7.6 goals below expected) hasn't helped. Any buyer would be getting a 34-goal scorer from last season whose chances still look sound.

Per Daily Faceoff, Toronto defenseman Jake McCabe left the Maple Leafs' game against the Blue Jackets with an injury. The outlet notes he has gone without a point through 10 games to start the season.

The scoreless start is less alarming than it sounds. McCabe's expected goals (the quality of chances from his own shots) are just 0.4 so far this season, so he is only 0.4 goals short of what those looks should have produced. His value was never offense. The bigger concern is that Toronto controls only 37.87 percent of the expected goals at five-on-five with him on the ice, and the team's share is 7.13 percentage points better when he sits. That makes him a tough fit as a top-pair defenseman playing 22:00 a night and killing penalties, and Toronto's overall 43 percent five-on-five share suggests the Leafs lean heavily on goalie play (6.6 goals saved above expected). Going by how the coach has used his players, Morgan Rielly (18:54 a night) is next in line for McCabe's minutes. McCabe has missed no games yet, so that is a projection, not a result.

If he misses time, the minutes are going by how the coach has used his players, not by games already played without him. Scott Laughton (14:40 a night) is next in line for his ice time, and Alex Turcotte, the busiest man on the second power-play unit, is the likeliest to move up.

The timing stings a little, because Markstrom has been better than his save percentage suggests. His .897 looks ordinary, but he has saved 1.28 goals more than expected so far this season (goals saved above expected measures how many goals a goalie prevented compared with an average goalie facing the same shots). Last year he was at minus 15.98 over 44 games, so this is a rebound, though six games is a small sample. FLA overall sits at 5-2-2 with 53.5% of the expected goals (the quality of chances, which is a better read on play than the score), and the team has scored 1.5 fewer goals than its chances warranted. The Panthers' goaltending as a group is 2.3 goals above expected, so the net has not been the problem. Their 56% expected goal share at five-on-five is the stronger signal. For fantasy owners, Markstrom is a hold only if the roster can absorb two weeks. The Panthers' underlying numbers say the team should stay steady, but whoever fills in has little room to slip.

The numbers so far this season give neither team much urgency to move them. Myers has no points in seven games for Dallas, and the Stars generate 44.34% of the 5-on-5 expected goals with him on the ice, which is 7.54 percentage points worse than when he sits. At 14.49 minutes a night, he is a depth defender whose results are not hurting him unfairly, since his own expected goals are just 0.13. Norris is a different case. His 5-on-5 share is a break-even 50.85%, but his 1.24 own expected goals against 1 goal points to a bit of bad finishing, not a bad process, and Buffalo's 4-3-1 start looks fine underneath, at 52.1% of total expected goals. His 0.84 model expected goals per 60 and last season's 13 goals in 44 games suggest the production is there to come. Both samples are tiny, so this is a read on the early picture, not a verdict.

stories.take:
The Athletic reports that David Perron has signed with the Dallas Stars for his 20th NHL season, and that he will play for the eighth team of his career.

The numbers suggest Dallas has a real reason to add scoring help. So far this season, the Stars are 4-3-1 with 9 points in 8 games, and they have created 51.3 percent of the expected goals, a measure of shot quality that tells you who had the better chances. That is a slight edge. At 5-on-5 it slips to 49 percent, so even-strength play has been roughly an even fight. The finishing is the problem: Dallas is 3.7 goals below what its chances should have produced. Goalie play has been the saving grace, with a goals saved above expected figure of 9.5, meaning the goaltending has stopped 9.5 more goals than an average goalie would have behind those shots. That cushion has carried the record, and it may not last. The power play is generating 0.75 expected goals per game, which leaves room for a veteran like Perron to help, while the penalty kill has allowed just 0.5 expected goals per game and looks sturdy. If Perron helps close the gap between chances and goals, Dallas could turn a goalie-driven start into something steadier.
